$comment: PINNED SCREEN PARAMETERS. Written before the screen was run against any stranger wallet, and
committed in their own commit so the ordering is the audit trail. Every number is anchored to a
measurement that already exists in this repository or in a committed scout report, and the
anchor is named in `justification`. Do not move a value to fit an output. If a value must
change, change it here, say why in the PR, and re-run Stage 0 first: a screen that no longer
reproduces the answers we already know is not ready to judge strangers.
SCOPE: this tool GATES on competence and SCORES ENTRY. It does not recommend, and it does not
score EXIT — see `stage2_entry`.
$versionNote: 5.1.0 adds the `dune` block and moves NO bar. Captain decision 156a: creation ENUMERATION —
'which mints did this wallet create' — becomes primary on Dune, and the Solana RPC creation
walk (keyless, or indexed through Helius) becomes its FALLBACK. Nothing about Stage 2 or
Stage 3 changes, and Helius stays primary and necessary for every transaction-level
measurement, including Stage 2's entry-cost leg, which reads meta.fee and pre/post balances
per transaction — Dune's decoded tables do not serve that and never will.
A run record persists `enumerationSource` per candidate, so a reader can tell which surface
answered without inferring it from the thresholds version.
5.0.0 adds the ENTRY COST bars — stage2_entry.minFieldHitRateNet, maxEntryCostPerSolStaked
and minPricedFraction, plus the whole stage2_cost block. Captain's standing ruling of
2026-08-02: fees are part of the entry window, and 'enterable' means enterable AFTER what it
costs to enter. Decision 136b adds the field's after-cost result.
A run record persists this string as `thresholdsVersion`, so a record written under 4.0.0 or
earlier was scored with the price of the seat UNMEASURED — which is a different question
from the one a 5.0.0 record answers, not a weaker answer to the same one.

$comment: Keyed, MadeOnSol, one request per candidate. A GATE, not a score: it asks whether a
deployer is competent, which is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. Stage 0 demonstrates
the gap empirically — it shows the gate PASSING the one deployer we know is not worth the
time.
The denominator is `profile.pump_tokens[].complete` and nothing else. Never `bonding_rate`,
`total_bonded`, `total_tokens_deployed`, `recent_bond_rate`, `recent_outcomes` or
`best_token_peak_mc`, which are trailing windows or stale; and never
/deployer-hunter/{wallet}/tokens, which is bonded-only and so has no denominator at all.

justification.completionRateSource: NOT A THRESHOLD — the field the other three bars are computed from, and the reasoning for it is this block's $comment at length: profile.pump_tokens[].complete agreed with our tape 67/67 on the completion flag with no in-window launch missing, while every published aggregate is a trailing ~7.5-day window their own alert text calls 'lifetime', and /deployer-hunter/{wallet}/tokens is bonded-only and so has no denominator at all. Named here as well because this file's contract is that the anchor is in `justification`.
justification.minTokens: MadeOnSol's own spec tells consumers to gate on labeled_tokens >= 3. That is far too low: on our subject deployer a 22-token window read 0.6818 against a true 0.4310, so a window of ~22 was enough to be wrong by 58% relative. 25 is the floor at which their sliding-window artefact stops being the whole measurement, and it is 8x their published gate. NAME THE POPULATION, THOUGH: that evidence is about the VENDOR'S TRAILING WINDOW, while rank.mjs compares `completion.tokens` of whatever history reading the run produced — by default the creation-derived merged listing, which is larger and therefore easier to clear than the window this figure was measured on. The bar is a 'worth scoring at all' filter rather than a claim about the deployer, so the mismatch is bounded, but the two are not the same count and no measurement fixes 25 against the merged one. It is NOT enough for a lifetime claim, which is why the span is reported alongside and why long-horizon consistency is reported UNMEASURED.
justification.minCompletionRate: 0.25 is MadeOnSol's own published 'good' tier lifetime bar. Our subject deployer's true lifetime rate is 0.4310 (239 launches, 103 bonded) and it is a genuinely competent operator, so a bar meaningfully below that admits the population we care about while excluding deployers that mostly fail.
justification.minSpanDays: A high rate earned inside a single day is a burst, not a record — and this bar measures exactly that: rank.mjs compares `completion.spanDays`, which is FIRST DEPLOY TO LAST DEPLOY over the gate's history reading, not time-to-bond. The two are not the same quantity and an earlier version of this entry justified the first with a distribution of the second, computed from `curve_last_tx_s`; that column is formally ruled a valid upper BOUND and not a usable timing (data/population-tape-2026-07-29/IMPORT.md, Corrections 4, median overshoot 8.85x), so the clause is withdrawn rather than re-derived and the column is not quoted here. The measured median graduation time on this operator is 1,042 s = 17.4 MINUTES (IMPORT.md, Corrections 5), so 14 days is orders of magnitude above what a launch needs to resolve: this bar exists to refuse a wallet whose whole history is one burst, not to wait for bonding. NOTE THE RESIDUAL GAP, which no span bar closes: a wallet that deploys most of its tokens in the last 48 hours of a 14-day span still clears this, and its unresolved launches then depress its completion rate — which errs towards rejection, the direction this tool prefers to fail in.

$comment: THE CANDIDATE DISCOVERY FEED — tools/deployer-screen/feed.mjs, documented in FEED.md.
A scheduled lane that surfaces deployers this project has NOT seen before, triages them on
the Stage 1 gate, and queues the survivors for the beatability screen. It supersedes the
re-open monitor (captain, 2026-08-02: a competent dev that tightened its own launch bot does
not loosen it again, so re-polling wallets already graded closed watches the one place a
window will not reopen; the opportunity is in the POPULATION, not the graveyard).
THESE BOUNDS EXIST BECAUSE THIS LANE RUNS FOREVER. Every other caller of the MadeOnSol key
is a one-off a human decided to spend. A scheduled lane is not, so an unbounded provider
call here is worse than anywhere else in the tool: it would drain the shared allowance on a
cron and the screen would find nothing left. The feed's per-run keyed cost is therefore
3 enumeration + at most gateBatch profile requests, and NOTHING else is keyed.
THE DAILY ARITHMETIC IS THE POINT AND IT IS DELIBERATELY A MINORITY SHARE:
maxKeyedRequestsPerRun 15 x runsPerDayAssumed 6 = 90 of the ~200/day Free-tier allowance,
worst case, leaving >=110 for screen.mjs. At the DEFAULT gateBatch of 6 it is 9 x 6 = 54.
Raising runsPerDayAssumed without lowering the per-run ceiling is how this lane silently
becomes the allowance's largest consumer — change both or neither.
THE FEED SPENDS NO KEYLESS REQUEST AT ALL. It grades on the ownership reading, which is one
keyed profile call, and does NOT walk the creation-derived history: that walk is ~100 RPC
requests per candidate at 2.5s apart, which no schedule can carry. The consequence is stated
rather than hidden — the ownership reading is biased TOWARDS REJECTION (README.md, 'Which
history the gate counts'), so a feed failure is recorded as `held`, never as a rejection, and
the standing count of held wallets is printed by every run. screen.mjs remains the authority.

justification.gateBatch: Six new wallets a run, six runs a day, is 36 gate readings a day for 54 keyed requests. The two committed screen runs surfaced 22 and 72 distinct wallets from one enumeration each — runs/2026-07-29-elite.json and runs/2026-08-02-good.json, field coverage.distinctWalletsSeeded, from 74 and 150 rows returned — so a first live run defers most of what it sees and drains the backlog over the following days, which is why nextGateBatch is FIFO. An earlier version of this entry said 61 and 84; neither figure appears in either record (61 is feed/ledger.json's standing `held` count, a different quantity over the union of both runs), and the argument holds at 72 as it did at 84. Lower it if the screen needs more of the allowance; it can only ever be lowered from the command line.
justification.maxGateBatch: The hard cap --gate cannot exceed. 12 keeps the worst-case per-run keyed cost at 15 and therefore the assumed daily cost at 90, under half the allowance. A bound a flag can widen is not a bound.
justification.maxKeyedRequestsPerRun: 3 enumeration + maxGateBatch 12. Enforced before the first request: a plan whose worst case does not fit is refused with nothing spent, exactly as screen.mjs refuses one.
justification.runsPerDayAssumed: NOT enforced by the tool — nothing here can see a cron table. It is the number the daily arithmetic above is computed against, and it is recorded so that a schedule which contradicts it is contradicting a written figure rather than an assumption. Six runs a day is four-hourly.
justification.seedLimit: The page size asked of each enumeration query. 50 is the maximum recent-bonds and leaderboard accept (their spec's 100 returns HTTP 400) and is what alerts is clamped to as well, so this is 'as much as the vendor will give for one request' rather than a tunable.
justification.dryStreakAlarm: Three consecutive live, completed runs with no new wallet — an aborted run surfaced nothing because it stopped, so it is skipped rather than counted. One dry run is ordinary: the vendor's pages overlap heavily between runs and at four-hourly cadence most of what comes back is yesterday's list. Three in a row is saturation of what this vendor exposes, and it exits non-zero so a scheduler notices. A dead feed that reads as a healthy quiet one is the exact failure this lane was told to make impossible.
justification.runHistoryKept: 60 run rows, i.e. ten days at the assumed cadence. Enough to see a yield trend and to compute the dry streak; bounded so a committed ledger does not grow without limit.

$comment: The captain's word was 'consistently'. MadeOnSol cannot answer it: their only
denominator-complete surface (profile.pump_tokens) is capped at 70 records and about 35 days.
Manufacturing a long-horizon claim from a 35-day window is exactly the defect we found in
their own aggregate, so the tool does not do it. Long-horizon consistency is reported as
UNMEASURED unless --consistency is passed, which pages a keyless pump.fun creator listing and
spends no quota.

justification.default: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch. Long-horizon consistency is UNMEASURED unless asked for, because the only denominator-complete vendor surface is a ~35-day window and manufacturing a lifetime claim from it is the defect this tool exists to refuse. See this block's $comment.
justification.optIn: NOT A MEASUREMENT — the flag that turns the pass on. It pages a keyless pump.fun creator listing and spends no vendor quota.
justification.minEpochs: AN UNMEASURED OPERATIONAL BOUND, stated as one. What the code computes is max(epoch rate) - min(epoch rate) across qualifying epochs (rank.mjs), and a spread over 2 points is just the two ends: 3 is the smallest count at which 'spread' describes a distribution rather than a difference. That is arithmetic about the statistic, not evidence about deployers — nothing in this repo measures how many 30-day epochs a completion rate needs to stabilise. What would justify a specific value: bucket the subject's own 239 committed launches into 30-day epochs and show at what epoch count the dispersion figure itself stops moving. That is computable offline from data/population-tape-2026-07-29/launches.csv today and has not been run. Until it is, this is a floor chosen for the shape of the statistic, and the consequence of being wrong is bounded — consistency FLAGS and never filters (see maxDispersion), and below this floor the tool reports UNMEASURED rather than estimating.
justification.minTokensPerEpoch: AN UNMEASURED OPERATIONAL BOUND, and the same arithmetic minFieldRoundTrips makes explicitly: a rate over n tokens moves by 1/n when one outcome changes, so at 12 a single bond or failure moves an epoch's rate by 8.3 points and a bucket thinner than that is noise wearing a percentage sign. 12 is chosen for that property, not measured — no committed measurement says a 30-day epoch of a real deployer needs 12 tokens to be readable, and the vendor's own profile cap (70 records over ~35 days) is the reason most candidates will have few qualifying epochs at all. The same offline bucketing of launches.csv proposed for minEpochs would justify or move it. A bucket below the floor does not qualify, so the failure direction is UNMEASURED rather than a wrong rate.
justification.epochDays: 30-day epochs are long enough that an epoch is not one week of luck, and short enough that a 6-month history yields the 3 required.
justification.maxDispersion: max(epoch rate) - min(epoch rate) > 0.35 FLAGS a deployer as streaky rather than excluding it. A flag, not a filter: the point of the exercise is that one hot window must not read as a record, and the reader is entitled to see the spread rather than have it silently applied.

$comment: Bounds for the creation-derived launch history — the walk that answers 'which tokens did this
wallet CREATE' instead of 'which tokens does it OWN NOW'. See creation.mjs for why the two
differ and for the on-chain observation that established it.
This walk is the expensive part of a run by an order of magnitude, because the only keyless
index that reaches a create transaction is the wallet's own signature index, and for a pump.fun
deployer that index is dominated by strangers' failed trades. Every bound here is therefore a
hard ceiling, and readCreatedHistory reports which one bit rather than truncating silently.
The walk covers a CONTIGUOUS WINDOW BACKWARDS FROM NOW. Inside it every creation is found;
outside it none is, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing and says so. A
create count read as a lifetime figure under any stopReason other than 'index-exhausted' is
wrong in the same direction as the vendor's sliding 'lifetime' window.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: Measured 2026-08-02: sustained keyless throughput against api.mainnet-beta is about 0.42 transactions/second, i.e. roughly one request per 2.4s including backoff, and a create is found by inspecting every SUCCEEDED signature in the wallet's index. The success fraction varies enormously between deployers — 1.7% on the busiest wallet screened, 99.7% on another — so the cost of a full history ranged from 7 minutes to 84 hours across the 12 wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json. 100 requests is a per-candidate ceiling that keeps a 12-candidate run inside about 50 minutes; on a quiet wallet it is the whole history, on a busy one it is a window of hours and the record says so. NOTE THE OTHER END OF THAT ARITHMETIC: at the 195-candidate cap it is 19,500 requests and ~13.5 HOURS, which is the dominant cost of a default run — --candidates N is the lever that bounds it, and --ownership-only skips it for a fast pass whose bias is stamped into the record. See CREATION-DERIVED.md for the per-wallet costs.
justification.maxSignaturePages: 200 pages is 200,000 signatures, past which no keyless walk is finishing inside a session. It exists so a wallet with an enormous index cannot turn the request ceiling into the only brake.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, and there is no measurement behind the number. pumpfun.mjs stops the walk at transactionsInspected >= this, but a transaction is inspected one getTransaction at a time (txBatchSize 1) from a client capped at maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate 100, so AT MOST ~100 transactions can ever be inspected for one candidate — 8000 is unreachable by a factor of ~80, and every real walk stops on 'request-ceiling' or 'index-exhausted' instead. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising the request ceiling does not silently remove the only bound on inspection work, and it is documented as unjustified rather than given a manufactured anchor: what would justify a value is a measured cost per inspected transaction against a wall-clock budget, which only exists for the REQUEST ceiling (see maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate, 0.42 tx/s measured 2026-08-02). Delete it or re-derive it if the request ceiling ever rises above it.
justification.txBatchSize: 1, and the 1 is measured. report.md 9.4 recorded batches of 5-8 getTransaction as sustainable, and that no longer holds: on 2026-08-02, fetching the same transactions at batch=1 took 58s with ZERO load-shed events, batch=4 took 76s with 7, and batch=8 took 110s with 11. Throughput was 0.42 tx/s at batch=1 and 0.36 tx/s at batch=8 — the endpoint weights each entry of a JSON-RPC batch against its limiter, so a batch of 8 spends 8 tokens and buys nothing but backoff. Batching is therefore actively harmful HERE TOO, exactly as it is on pump.fun's keyless endpoints. The client still supports batching, capped at 8, because the endpoint's behaviour is the vendor's to change and re-measuring is cheaper than rebuilding.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: 1,400ms is the documented floor, but a 200-request run at that pace on 2026-08-02 took over 890 seconds instead of the expected 280 — the endpoint was shedding load and the retry backoff was paying for it. 2,500ms is the observed rate at which that stops happening, so it is faster in wall-clock than the nominally quicker setting. api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction, and two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout, so this is one queue with one request in flight.

$comment: CREATION ENUMERATION, PRIMARY SURFACE. Captain decision 156a, 2026-08-03. The same question
creation_walk and creation_walk_helius answer — 'which mints did this wallet CREATE' — read
off Dune's decoded pump.fun creation events instead of walked out of a signature index.
tools/deployer-screen/dune.mjs owns the method; CREATION-DERIVED.md section 8 owns the
reproduction and the measured cost.
THE SURFACE IS A UNION AND THE UNION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: pump_evt_createevent UNION
pump_call_create, deduped by mint. pump_call_create ALONE returns ZERO rows for our subject
(it decodes only the original Create; this deployer uses CreateV2). pump_call_create_v2 ALONE
is not backfilled before ~2026-04-28 and silently misses 101 of our 239 launches, `maxxing`
included. Attribution keys on "user"/account_user, the SIGNER — never on `creator`, which is
a settable CreateV2 argument that six bot-signed mints use to name our subject, inflating the
EVERY DUNE-DERIVED COUNT SHIPS WITH ITS OWN COVERAGE PROBE, and that is the binding condition
of the decision rather than a nicety. Decoded tables have SILENT START DATES: they return a
confident, well-formed, complete-looking answer that is simply wrong before their first row,
with nothing in the response saying so. Same failure shape as a truncated backwards walk in
pumpfun.mjs and the same direction: plausible and silent. dune.mjs -> assessCoverage refuses
a reading that reaches outside the probe, and a refused reading FALLS BACK to the walk — it is
never published as a measured count.
SPEND. Free tier, 2,500 credits/month, SHARED with whatever else holds the key, and nothing
here tracks the month — the monthly arithmetic is the operator's, exactly as it is for Helius.
A FAILED EXECUTION IS STILL BILLED AND IS TERMINAL: client.mjs -> DuneClient never retries
one, and no code may wrap a retry around it. Budget from BILLED credits, not
execution_cost_credits, which understates by ~3.5x because retrieving results is ~71% of the
bill at ~20 credits/MB.

justification.creationQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved query the enumeration executes, pinned so a run names the surface it read. dune.mjs -> CREATION_SQL holds that query's SQL byte for byte and assertSavedQueryMatches compares the two BEFORE spending an execution, so a saved query edited from a browser fails the run loudly instead of returning a different measurement under the same name. Reused rather than created: it is the query data/slot-zero-dune-evaluate/report.md section 7 designates as the production shape, upgraded in place from event-only to the union, because the free tier allows only 10 private queries and the account holds 10.
justification.coverageQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved coverage probe, pinned for the same reason and verified the same way against COVERAGE_SQL. It is the scout's own coverage query (report.md section 2) widened to carry min/max block time beside the monthly counts. It probes THREE tables while the enumeration reads TWO: pump_call_create_v2 is included precisely so the probe's own output demonstrates the boundary that disqualifies it, rather than this file asserting it in prose.
justification.maxExecutionsPerRun: 2, and the 2 is the exact plan rather than a round number: one execution for the enumeration, and at most one more to re-execute the coverage probe when the cached one has gone stale. Nothing else in a run may execute. An execution is BILLED WHETHER OR NOT IT SUCCEEDS and is never retried, so this is the bound on the only unrecoverable spend the Dune leg has. MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this account: the enumeration of 5 wallets / 482 rows cost 0.919 execution credits and 1.919 billed; the coverage probe cost 0.751 execution credits and 0.751 billed. AT THE 195-CANDIDATE CAP the execution cost barely moves — scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter, measured at 5 and at 20 — and what scales is bytes returned, which maxResultRows bounds. NOTHING HERE TRACKS THE MONTH: the tool is stateless between runs and cannot see what the allowance has already paid for, so this bounds ONE run and the monthly arithmetic is the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxRequestsPerRun: Requests bound the WALL CLOCK and the polite use of a shared host; maxExecutionsPerRun bounds the money, and the two are separate ceilings because a poll loop that spent an execution's worth of budget on status checks would be counting the wrong thing. The arithmetic: each of the two possible executions costs 1 SQL-verification GET + 1 execute + up to maxPollAttempts 40 status polls + 1 results read = 43, so 2 x 43 = 86, and the remaining 14 are the retry headroom (every read is retried at most once, and each attempt counts). 100 is that sum. MEASURED: both executions on 2026-08-03 completed in 6-9 s, i.e. 2-3 polls, so a real run spends about 8 requests and the ceiling is a backstop rather than a budget.
justification.maxResultRows: 20,000 rows, and THE UNIT THAT MATTERS IS BYTES rather than rows, because results are billed at ~20 credits/MB and that is ~71% of the bill. MEASURED 2026-08-03: the union enumeration returns ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes) after the create transaction and the graduation timestamp were dropped from the SELECT — they halved the payload and the tool reads neither. So this ceiling is ~1.94 MB, about 39 credits, or 1.6% of the free monthly allowance in one read. WHAT A REAL RUN COSTS AGAINST IT: at the 195-candidate cap and a median deployer history of ~50 launches, ~9,750 rows is ~0.95 MB, about 20 credits — roughly 125 full-cap runs a month. The ceiling REFUSES rather than pages: an unbounded read is an unbounded bill, and a paged one would spend the allowance discovering how big the answer was.
justification.pollIntervalMs: 3,000 ms between status polls. MEASURED 2026-08-03: the two executions finished in 6 s and 9 s, so a run polls two or three times. Polling faster would buy at most a couple of seconds against a leg that replaces a walk measured in hours, and it is a shared free-tier host. Polling is a READ and costs no execution credit, but every poll counts against maxRequestsPerRun, which is what stops a slow execution turning into an unbounded loop.
justification.maxPollAttempts: 40 polls at 3,000 ms is 120 s, against the 6-9 s the two committed executions actually took — roughly 13x the observed worst. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE, and it is stated as an operational bound rather than dressed up: nothing in this repo measures the tail of Dune execution latency, because two executions is not a distribution. What would justify a value: execution durations over a month of scheduled runs, which the run record's dune block will accumulate. The failure direction is the safe one — running out of polls abandons the Dune leg and falls back to the RPC walk, and the execution is billed either way, so the cost of being wrong here is bounded by one execution.
justification.minIntervalMs: 250 ms between request starts, and NO MEASUREMENT OF THIS HOST BACKS IT. It is a courtesy floor on a free tier, carried across from creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200 ms, which WAS measured, on a different vendor) and rounded up rather than down. A real run issues about 8 requests, so the pacing costs ~2 s of a run measured in minutes and buying a measurement of it would be spending a shared allowance to tune something that is not a cost. What would justify a value: a pacing ladder against Dune's status endpoint recording shed events per rung, which is exactly what was done for Helius and has not been done here.
justification.maxCoverageLagMs: 6 hours. The probe cannot vouch for a period it does not reach, and the recent end is precisely where a live screen looks — a deployer that launched this morning is the one a discovery feed just surfaced. Dune's own freshness was measured by the scout at ~3-4 minutes (report.md section 6, item 8), so 6 hours is about 100x the vendor's lag and is not a tight bar; what it actually bounds is OUR cache, since the probe defaults to a cached read that could be arbitrarily old. THE FAILURE IS REPAIRED RATHER THAN INHERITED: when staleness is the ONLY thing wrong, dune.mjs re-executes the probe once, which is the second of the two budgeted executions. A structural refusal — a missing table, a month with no rows — is not retried, because asking the same question again returns the same answer.
justification.refreshProbeByDefault: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch, and it is `false` because the probe is PARAMETERLESS and therefore has a cached answer that costs no execution at all. Re-executing it every run would spend the binding budget on a figure that moves by one row per second. `--dune-refresh-probe` makes it explicit, and staleness re-executes it anyway (see maxCoverageLagMs), so the default cannot silently publish a count over coverage nobody checked.

$comment: The SAME measurement as creation_walk, over an indexed provider instead of a raw signature
scan. It is used when HELIUS_API_KEY is set; with the key unset the creation_walk block above
governs and the run is byte-for-byte what it was before this block existed.
Helius getTransactionsForAddress applies `status: succeeded` server-side and returns the
transaction bodies in the same call, so it collapses BOTH halves of the keyless walk — page
signatures, then one getTransaction per survivor — into one request per 1,000 transactions.
PLAN: Helius Developer, $49/month, 10,000,000 credits/month, 50 requests/second (their
pricing page, read 2026-08-03). getTransactionsForAddress in `full` mode bills 10 CREDITS PER
100 TRANSACTIONS RETURNED, rounded up, 10 minimum; getMultipleAccounts is a standard method at
1 credit. The key is UNSHARED — it belongs to this research lane alone (captain, 2026-08-03),
so the whole allowance is this tool's and no other consumer can be starved by a heavy run.
CREDITS ARE THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, NOT WALL CLOCK, and that is the inversion this block
exists to record. The keyless walk was bounded by time: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s
is 13.5 hours. Here the same 195 candidates at the worst measured per-candidate cost is about
46 minutes — and 1,014,000 credits, which is 10.14% of a month's allowance in one run. DO NOT
'CORRECT' THAT 46 DOWN TO THE 32.5 THE PACING FLOOR IMPLIES: 195 x 50 pages x 200ms is the
naive arithmetic, and this walk is LATENCY-BOUND below ~250ms of enforced interval. The
2026-08-03 full-mode ladder (20 requests a rung, one in flight) measured 962/490/301/251/257 ms
per request at enforced intervals of 1000/500/250/100/0 ms, i.e. a floor of ~250-260ms set by
response latency (p50 ~220ms) with ~50ms of overhead once the interval dominates. At the pinned
200ms a page really costs ~280ms, so 195 x 50 x 280ms = 45.5 min. render.mjs prints the same
figure from MEASURED_PAGE_CYCLE_MS rather than from the interval. So the
ceiling below is stated in credits, and the page count is a SEPARATE bound rather than the
same one restated: since the per-page guard reserves the curve-classification pass on top of
a whole page, the credit ceiling carries headroom the page cap does not, and the page cap is
what binds first. See the two justifications for the arithmetic.

justification.maxCreditsPerCandidate: MEASURED 2026-08-03 against the only population where both readings exist: the twelve wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json, every one of them enumerated to EXHAUSTION. Succeeded-transaction counts per wallet: 168, 211, 1007, 1026, 2136, 2989, 3344, 4749, 6378, 7791, 46815, 49367 — median ~3,167, max 49,367. At 10 credits per 100 returned that is 20, 30, 110, 110, 220, 300, 340, 480, 640, 780, 4690, 4940 credits for a COMPLETE history, median ~320, max 4,940, and 12,660 for all twelve together. THE CEILING IS 5,200 RATHER THAN 5,000 BECAUSE THE PER-PAGE GUARD COSTS MORE THAN A PAGE, and the arithmetic has to be stated or the next reader re-derives 5,000 and reintroduces the defect: a page is only STARTED when a whole page's worst case still fits ALONGSIDE the curve-classification reservation, and that reservation is creditsForCurveReads(creates.length + pageLimit) = ceil(n/100) + 1, whose floor at pageLimit 1,000 is 11. So the guard demands 100 + 11 = 111 credits free, not 100. At 5,000 the walk could start a page only while 111 remained, which after 49 full pages leaves 100 and stops on `credit-ceiling` at 49,000 transactions — SHORT OF THE 49,367 OF 6Wg4aeZ2, the very wallet the ceiling was sized against, so the population's largest history would have truncated while this text claimed it did not. 5,200 affords 51 data pages, past both the 50-page cap and that largest history, so every wallet in the measured population walks its whole index rather than a window — which is the coverage this route buys and the reason the ceiling is not set at the median. The reservation itself is not negotiable: CREATION-DERIVED.md §4 owns it, and a walk that spends its last unit finding one more creation has bought a launch it must then score as NOT bonded, deflating the very rate the walk was widening. The failure direction is the one the keyless walk already has and already reports: a wallet costlier than 5,200 credits stops on `credit-ceiling`, its covered window is a window and says so, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing beyond it. WHAT WOULD MOVE IT: a wallet measured above 49,367 succeeded transactions whose reading the gate needs whole, or a change to pageLimit or to creditsForCurveReads, both of which move the 111.
justification.maxCreditsPerRun: 11% of the Developer plan's 10,000,000 monthly credits, chosen so that the DEFAULT plan is admissible and the arithmetic is visible: maxCandidates 195 x maxCreditsPerCandidate 5,200 = 1,014,000 worst case, which fits under 1,100,000 with margin. THE TWO CEILINGS ARE COUPLED AND MUST MOVE TOGETHER — that is the whole reason this one changed: screen.mjs refuses a plan whose worst case exceeds this value BEFORE its first request, so raising the per-candidate ceiling from 5,000 to 5,200 while leaving this at 1,000,000 would have made EVERY default run refuse to start (1,014,000 > 1,000,000). That worst case is ~10.14% of the monthly allowance, so roughly nine worst-case full-cap runs fit in a month, and the measured EXPECTED cost is far lower — at the median per-candidate 320 credits a full 195-candidate run is about 62,400 credits, i.e. 0.62% of the month, so roughly 160 such runs would fit. THE POINT IS THE REFUSAL, NOT THE NUMBER: screen.mjs computes the worst case before its first request and refuses a plan that does not fit, so raising either per-candidate bound or the candidate cap without raising this one stops the run BEFORE it spends rather than part-way through, which is the same rule the keyed and keyless ceilings already enforce. NOTHING HERE TRACKS THE MONTH: this tool holds no state between runs and cannot see what the allowance has already paid for, so this bounds ONE run and the monthly arithmetic is the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxPagesPerCandidate: NOT the same bound as maxCreditsPerCandidate any more, and the correction is the point: it USED to be an exact restatement — a full page of pageLimit 1,000 costs exactly 100 credits, so 5,000 credits was precisely 50 pages and neither could bind before the other. That stopped being true when the credit ceiling rose to 5,200 to clear the 111-credit per-page guard (see maxCreditsPerCandidate). At 5,200 the credit ceiling affords 51 data pages, so THE PAGE CAP IS NOW WHAT BINDS FIRST and the credit ceiling carries the guard's headroom behind it. 50 is kept rather than raised because 50 pages is 50,000 transactions, still above the largest history measured (49,367), so the measured population still walks whole; and the page cap exists at all because the walk's loop counts pages, and because a future pageLimit change would otherwise silently move the page bound with no line saying so.
justification.pageLimit: 1000 is the endpoint's own maximum and it is enforced rather than documented-only: `limit: 5000` returns HTTP 200 carrying {"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"Bad request: Invalid limit: You can only request up to 1000 transactions at a time…"}} (measured 2026-08-03). Asking for less would multiply both the request count and the 10-credit-per-page MINIMUM — a walk at limit 100 pays the same 10 credits for a tenth of the answer — so the endpoint's cap is also the cheapest setting.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, stated as one, exactly like creation_walk.maxTransactionsPerCandidate. 50 pages x 1,000 = 50,000, so this equals the page bound and no walk can reach it first. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising maxPagesPerCandidate or pageLimit does not silently remove the only bound expressed in the unit the parser actually works in. No measurement fixes it beyond the page arithmetic above, and inventing one would be worse than saying so.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this endpoint, this plan, this client shape (one request in flight). A pacing ladder over getTransactionsForAddress against the busiest measured wallet — full mode at 1000/500/250/100/0 ms, 20 requests a rung, and signatures mode at 500/200/100/50/0 ms, 30 a rung — recorded ZERO shed events and zero JSON-RPC errors at EVERY rung, including 0 ms. Throughput saturated well below the plan's documented 50 req/s because the walk is latency-bound, not limit-bound: full pages returned p50 ~220 ms and topped out at 3.98 req/s (interval 100) against 3.89 (interval 0), signature pages at 7.54 against 7.38. A separate concurrency probe of 150 simultaneous requests observed 161 req/s with all 150 answered 200, so the documented ceiling was never reached at any pacing this client can produce serially. 200 ms is therefore NOT a shed-avoidance figure — nothing shed — it is a courtesy floor with an order of magnitude of headroom under the documented 50 req/s, and it costs about 17% of wall clock against the fastest rung on a leg that now takes seconds. THIS IS THE FREE ENDPOINT'S OPPOSITE and the contrast is the point: creation_walk.rpcMinIntervalMs is 2,500 ms because api.mainnet-beta sheds a quarter of what it is asked for and the nominally faster 1,400 ms measured SLOWER once backoff was counted. BATCHING IS NOT USED AND WAS NOT RE-MEASURED, because it no longer applies: this route issues one request per 1,000 transactions instead of one per transaction, so there is nothing left to batch. The JSON-RPC batching finding recorded against api.mainnet-beta (58s at batch=1 with zero shed, 110s at batch=8 with eleven) is untouched and still governs the keyless fallback.

$comment: Hard bounds, enforced in code. There is no flag that disables one.
CAPTAIN'S INSTRUCTION, 2026-08-02: 'There is no current free method to save on the madeonsol
key request limits ... use all free tier daily quota as needed if it gets results.' These
bounds are therefore the FULL Free-tier daily allowance (~200 requests/day), not a fraction
of it. An earlier quarter-allowance ceiling of 45 was this tool's own caution, never a
captain instruction, and it is WITHDRAWN — do not reintroduce it or re-derive it: there is no
free substitute for this data, so an unspent allowance buys nothing and only leaves questions
unanswered.
The conditional binds: 'if it gets results'. This authorises sizing a run by what the
question needs. It does NOT authorise sweeping, idle retrying, or re-running to re-evidence a
side observation. A run that cannot say in advance what it will answer does not get the
allowance.
SCOPE: this relaxation is MadeOnSol ONLY. The SolanaTracker / CoinGecko keys are shared with
production and the standing 'do not waste the quota that is production quota too' is
unchanged, as is the keyless pump.fun pacing below, which bounds a shared public resource for
an entirely different reason.
HELIUS IS NO LONGER IN THAT LIST (captain, 2026-08-03): its key is UNSHARED and belongs to
this research lane alone, so the whole 10M monthly allowance is this tool's and no other
consumer can be starved by a heavy run. It is metered on its own terms in
creation_walk_helius, in CREDITS rather than requests, because that is what the vendor bills.
The burst limit is NOT relaxed either: ~10/minute is a rate the vendor enforces, not a
self-imposed caution, so keyedMinIntervalMs stays.

justification.maxKeyedRequests: 200 is the whole Free-tier daily allowance as measured (see tools/deployer-screen/README.md). Enumeration costs 3 (recent-bonds, alerts, leaderboard) and the gate costs 1 per candidate, so the 195-candidate cap costs 198 worst case and the remaining 2 are the retry headroom. A run whose PLANNED worst case exceeds this is refused before its first request rather than allowed to die part-way through. STAGE 2 ADDS NOTHING TO THIS: it reuses the profile Stage 1 already fetched and spends no keyed request of its own.
justification.maxCandidates: 195 = 200 - 3 enumeration - 2 retry headroom, i.e. the cap is whatever the allowance leaves rather than a judgement about how many deployers are worth grading. It is also well above what the three enumeration queries can surface (50 + 50 + 50 rows, heavily overlapping and then pre-filtered — screen.mjs caps the page limit at 50 and seed.mjs then clamps alerts to the same 50, so the vendor's 100-row alerts ceiling is never asked for; both committed runs show 50, and an earlier version of this entry read 50 + 100 + 50, which overstates what enumeration can reach and therefore understates the headroom), so the DEFAULT run grades everything it surfaces and coverage truncation becomes the exception it is supposed to be.
justification.keyedMinIntervalMs: Free tier bursts at ~10/minute. 6.5s between request starts keeps a run under that with margin, and margin matters because the allowance is shared. This is the vendor's rate limit, not our caution, so raising the daily bounds does not touch it. A full 198-request run therefore takes about 21 minutes, which is the intended cost of respecting the burst limit — but THAT IS NO LONGER THE RUN'S WALL CLOCK AND MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE. The default history source is creation-derived, and the Solana RPC walk dominates everything else by an order of magnitude: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s is ~13.5 HOURS on its own. Add ~21 minutes keyed, ~26 for the gate's ownership listing on frontend-api-v3, ~50 for Stage 2 on swap-api, up to ~50 more for Stage 2's cost leg (stage2_cost, 3 x 400 requests at the same 2.5s, and it SHARES this limiter rather than adding a second queue), and a further ~19.5 with --consistency, and a full default run at the candidate cap is ABOUT 16 HOURS end to end, or ~16.5 with --consistency. An earlier version of this note said 47 minutes; it predated the creation walk and was wrong by a factor of twenty. DO NOT KILL A DEFAULT RUN FOR STILL GOING AFTER AN HOUR. The liveness signal is not the same on every leg: the keyed and frontend-api-v3 clients print one line per request, but the creation walk would emit ~20,000 of those, so it prints a PERIODIC HEARTBEAT — the first request of each candidate and then every tenth, i.e. a line roughly every 25 seconds at this walk's 2.5s pacing, showing that candidate's spend against maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate. Watch that counter rather than expecting a line per request, and use --candidates N to bound the run (the RPC leg is N x 100 x 2.5s) or --ownership-only to skip the walk entirely for a fast pass whose bias towards rejection is stamped into the record. renderDryRun prints this arithmetic for whatever flags are actually passed.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: frontend-api-v3.pump.fun — the gate's ownership listing and the --consistency creator walk, which share one client. It does NOT govern the Stage 2 fill walk, which has its own pinned pacing (`stage2_entry.keylessMinIntervalMs`) because it reaches a different host that behaves differently. THIS VALUE IS A CONSERVATIVE CARRY-OVER, NOT A MEASUREMENT OF THE ENDPOINT IT GOVERNS, and the correction matters: the ~0.5 requests/second figure this was originally justified by was measured against api.mainnet-beta.solana.com, and the June report's own spend table records BOTH swap-api.pump.fun and frontend-api-v3.pump.fun as NOT CONTACTED — so it was never a pump.fun measurement at all. It is kept because it is conservative and because frontend-api-v3 has shed nothing in this tool's use of it; if that host is ever measured, this number should be re-derived from that measurement rather than from a different host's. Either way it bounds a shared public resource rather than expressing our own caution, so the MadeOnSol relaxation does not touch it. The RETRY COUNT is a separate question and is not this bound: a keyless request is retried on a 429 or a 5xx, and each attempt counts against maxKeylessRequests.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: A PER-CLIENT CEILING, NOT A RUN TOTAL, and the distinction is what the code enforces: screen.mjs builds TWO independent keyless clients, and this value bounds only the general one (frontend-api-v3). Stage 2 runs on its own client under its own `stage2_entry.maxKeylessRequests` of 432, which this number neither contains nor constrains, so the enforced combined worst case is 1,400 + 432 = 1,832 requests. 1,400 is sized to COVER the candidate cap rather than to bound it, and it is sized for what the code now actually spends on this client, which is TWO passes and not one. The GATE reads the ownership listing it merges the creation window with, up to 4 pages PER CANDIDATE (screen.mjs LISTING_PAGES_FOR_MERGE); the --consistency pass then costs up to 3 pages per gate SURVIVOR, and every candidate can be one. So 195 candidates cost 195 x 4 = 780 for the gate plus 195 x 3 = 585 for consistency = 1,365 worst case, and the remaining 35 are the retry headroom. The earlier 600 was justified on the consistency pass alone and was already exceeded by gating at the default candidate cap. A keyless ceiling below the plan would make the tool stop looking part-way through a run it had already paid for in KEYED quota, and an unmeasured candidate is not a measured one — so screen.mjs now also REFUSES a plan whose keyless worst case does not fit, before its first request, exactly as it does for the keyed one. Raising the count does not lean harder on pump.fun — keylessMinIntervalMs is unchanged, so what it buys is wall-clock time and nothing else: 1,365 requests at 2s is ~45.5 minutes, of which ~26 is the gate's own 780 pages. That is a minority of the run's wall clock rather than the whole of it — see keyedMinIntervalMs, where the creation walk's ~13.5 hours puts a full default run at ABOUT 16 HOURS (13.54 h RPC + ~21 min keyed + ~26 min gate listing + ~50 min Stage 2 + ~50 min the cost leg = 15.97 h; an earlier version of this sentence said 15 and contradicted the 16 four lines above it). The June report sustained 460 consecutive keyless requests at 1.4s apart with zero shedding. These are pump.fun's free endpoints — no key, no vendor allowance, and no shared quota is touched by any of it.

$comment: ACTIVE. This is the `stage2_seam` block of thresholds v2.0.0, promoted in place — the two
values it reserved were pinned by the stage-0/1 lane BEFORE this lane existed to apply them,
and they are carried over unchanged with their original justification. That ordering is the
audit trail and it is the reason the block was not rewritten: a bar derived after seeing the
output it judges is not a bar. See git history for the superseded block verbatim.
What Stage 2 answers, from the captain's brief verbatim: 'Can I beat the dev and all other
wallets sniping the same tokens created by the dev currently?' — the ENTRY half of it.
(1) ENTRY ROOM: how much of the opening window the dev and its own cohort take before an
outsider is filled. The method of slot-zero-june-regime-change/report.md 5.1, 'the
operation's share of the curve's bottom'. In the captain's own framing, which is the
one the docs keep: this measures HOW BADLY CONFIGURED THE DEV'S OWN LAUNCH BOT IS.
(2) THE FIELD: what every OTHER sniping wallet on those same tokens achieved — fill, queue
position, and realised P&L. The question is whether WE beat them, so the competition is
measured and never assumed.
Both are keyless, from pump.fun fills. Stage 2 spends NO keyed request: it reuses the mint
list from the profile Stage 1 already fetched.
REPORTED AS DISTRIBUTIONS PLUS A HIT RATE, NEVER A MEAN. A standing captain bar for this
class of claim. Sniper outcomes are heavy-tailed on both sides, so a mean describes nobody.
NOT SCORED HERE, AND NO EXIT SIGNAL MAY REACH AN ENTRY NUMBER: exit feasibility (when the dev
sells relative to mint and to outsider inflow, whether the trigger is a SIZE and therefore
caps our position because our own buy counts towards it, and whether an outsider could have
exited first) is stage 3's separate deliverable. The prediction-grading loop is another lane
again. Room to enter is not room to leave, and one blended number cannot be read back apart.

justification.active: NOT A MEASUREMENT — the switch that says this block is live rather than reserved. It was `false` while the block was `stage2_seam` and the bars below were pinned before the lane existed to apply them; see this block's $comment for why that ordering is the audit trail.
justification.minRoomLeft: CARRIED UNCHANGED from thresholds v2.0.0 `stage2_seam.reservedMinRoomLeft`, pinned before this lane existed. Anchored on the only regime this project has MEASURED as profitable for create-slot outsiders. June report 5.1 puts the operation's share of the curve's bottom at 0.451 before 2026-06-04 (room 0.549) and PRINTS 0.768 after (room 0.232) — but that cell is quoted here as the PUBLISHED FIGURE, not as a measurement: it is the rank-43/44 order statistic of its own 89-launch series, whose median is 0.771 (room 0.229), and 0.771 is what this repo pins (captain decision 135c; the decomposition is in data/population-tape-2026-07-29/IMPORT.md -> 'Corrections'). The correction is 0.003 of share and moves nothing at this bar. 6.1 puts create-slot outsiders at +6.54 then +1.79 SOL per launch, and later entrants at +5.43 then -0.74. WHERE 0.55 SITS, CORRECTED 2026-08-02: an earlier version of this entry said 'room >= 0.55 is the pre-step regime', and that is false by 0.0008 — the May-only cut of 5.1 reads operation share 0.450771, i.e. room 0.549229, which FAILS this bar. The committed changepoint anchor is the one to read: analysis/window-population/measure.mjs — offline, in this repo, re-run 2026-08-02 — puts the OPEN regime (2026-03-12 to 2026-06-03, 129 launches, the only stretch a blind changepoint scan measures as paying create-slot outsiders, per-launch ROI p50 0.341) at operation share T1 p50 0.413, i.e. room 0.587. So 0.55 sits BETWEEN the two: inside the open regime and marginally above its tightest month, which means a deployer that merely matched May would be refused. That is the conservative direction — the bar cannot manufacture a false positive — and the value does not move.
justification.minLaunchesSampled: A BUDGET BOUND, NOT A STATISTICAL ONE, and it is documented as one because it is one (captain decision 141a, 2026-08-02). 8 is the largest sample the Stage 2 request ceiling affords — maxCandidatesScored 3 x maxLaunchesPerCandidate 8 x maxRequestsPerLaunch 18 = 432 = maxKeylessRequests — so what fixes it is the request arithmetic and nothing about the shape of a distribution. THE EVIDENCE RUNS THE OTHER WAY AND IS RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN OMITTED: the smallest per-launch bucket the June report was willing to state a quartile spread over is era B at n = 20 (slot-zero-june-regime-change/report.md 6.2, 'Per-launch non-cohort create-slot return per SOL, distribution across launches'), so a distribution over 8 launches is thinner than any spread this project has published, and A VERDICT RESTING ON 8 LAUNCHES IS CORRESPONDINGLY WEAKER EVIDENCE. An earlier version of this entry cited that bucket as the anchor for 8 and misquoted it as 22 — 22 is the era's launch count in the same report's three-era split table, which states no quartiles at all. The reader's recourse is in the record: every run record carries entry.launchesSampled, so what a verdict was computed over is visible rather than assumed. The floor cannot be raised on its own — it equals maxLaunchesPerCandidate, so raising it to 20 would need 3 x 20 x 18 = 1,080 Stage 2 requests and ~2.1 h of swap-api wall clock per run, and Stage 0 FAILS at >= 20 today because the known-negative control is scored over the last maxLaunchesPerCandidate launches. Captain decision 141a keeps 8 and rewrites this justification; it does not move the value.
justification.minFieldRoundTrips: A hit rate is the headline number of the field leg, and one over a handful of round trips is noise wearing a percentage sign. 10 is the floor at which a single outcome cannot move the rate by more than 10 points (1/10 exactly). Below it the field is reported UNMEASURED rather than estimated. IT GOVERNS TWO DIFFERENT POPULATIONS AND BOTH ARE MEANT: entry.mjs applies it to the CLOSED round trips of the gross leg, and again to the smaller set of closed round trips whose whole window was PRICED on-chain for the net leg. The same 1/n argument fixes both, and the second is necessarily the smaller — which is the conservative side, since a net reading over too few pairs is refused rather than estimated.
justification.minFieldHitRateNet: THE SAME BAR AS minFieldHitRateGross AND THE SAME VETO, now over a real measurement instead of an upper bound (captain decision 136b). Below 0.5 the field loses money more often than not AFTER what it paid, which is conclusive; above it nothing whatsoever is established, because measured cost is itself a LOWER bound — a landing tip paid in a separate transaction of the same bundle is not in it and is not in this repo's ground truth either. So the net figure is still an upper bound on what anyone took and still cannot EARN a verdict. Re-derived from the committed tape 2026-08-02 on our own subject's create-slot outsiders, matched to the on-chain cost table, over the GATED population Stage 0's verifyOnChainCostReproduction now prices — proven create-slot openings only, the same launches scoreEntry scores: 618 closed pairs priced end to end, gross hit rate 0.7379 against a NET 0.6117, and 81 of them flip from positive to negative. Post-break alone: 460 pairs, gross 0.7630, NET 0.6478, median gross +0.1157 SOL against a median NET +0.0482. That gap is what this bar now sees and the gross bar could not. (With the unproven openings left in, which is what this check measured before 2026-08-02: 631 pairs, 0.7401 gross against 0.6070 net, 87 flips; post-break 473 pairs, 0.7653 against 0.6406. Every run prints both, so the difference is auditable rather than asserted.)
justification.maxEntryCostPerSolStaked: PINNED ON MEASUREMENT, and the measurement is the create-slot half of the same reproduction. Entry cost is a wallet's real lamport outflow in its create-slot transaction less the swap-quote SOL it committed there, so it is the fee (base and priority), the venue fee, the rent, the execution difference and any tip paid inside that transaction. THE UNIT THIS BAR IS COMPARED AGAINST IS THE PER-LAUNCH MEDIAN, not the pooled per-entry one (captain decision 140a): every scored launch contributes its own median entry and exactly one observation, so a launch with dozens of priced entrants cannot outvote a launch with one. entry.mjs computes both — entryCostPerSolStakedByLaunch is what the verdict reads, entryCostPerSolStaked is the finer-grained per-entry evidence reported beside it — and a test pins the gate to the per-launch unit. THE DENOMINATOR IS THE SEAT, NOT THE WHOLE STAKE, and the name understates that: the per-entry ratio is entryCostSol / FieldEntrant.createSlotFillSol — the entrant's own create-slot curve buy — and NOT its whole-window FieldEntrant.stakeSol. On the committed tape the two coincide for the median entrant (stakeSol / createSlotFillSol reads p50 1.000, p90 1.000, max 47.63 over 757 priced entries), and the seat is the smaller denominator, so the implemented ratio is the LARGER one and this bar is the easier one to trip — conservative, which is the direction the cost leg must fail in. Re-derived 2026-08-02 from the same population Stage 0's verifyOnChainCostReproduction prices, which since 2026-08-02 is the GATED one — proven create-slot openings only, matching what scoreEntry itself scores (data/population-tape-2026-07-29/onchain_create_slot_pnl.csv, 110 launches, 757 create-slot entries): the PER-LAUNCH median is 0.0389 SOL per SOL staked, p90 0.0985, and the WORST LAUNCH ON THE TAPE IS 0.3311; pooled over the 757 individual entries the median is 0.0369, p75 0.0812, p90 0.1970. Post-break alone (78 launches, 492 entries): per-launch median 0.0354, p90 0.0571, worst launch 0.1361; per-entry median 0.0292. Leaving the unproven openings in — the population this check used to price — reads 113 / 775 and a per-launch median of 0.0388, i.e. 0.0001 CHEAPER, which is why the gated figure is the one quoted. The bar is 0.12, and what fixes it there is the field's own gross return over that same gated population: the median closed round trip returned 0.1246 SOL per SOL staked gross (460 pairs — the same 460 minFieldHitRateGross names below). A seat priced at 0.12 therefore costs essentially the whole of the gross prize, and since gross is an upper bound the median entrant cannot clear it — that is arithmetic, not a preference. The bar sits inside the observed range rather than above it, so it is not decorative: the worst-priced launch this project has ever measured would trip it. NOTE THE DIRECTION OF THE ERROR: an out-of-transaction landing tip is NOT in the numerator, so the measured price of the seat is a LOWER bound and this bar is harder to trip than the truth warrants. That is the optimistic direction, which is why the cost leg is a gate and never a pass.
justification.minPricedFraction: 0.8 of the create-slot field must be priced on-chain before any after-cost reading may stand. This is the coverage floor behind rule 1 of the ruling — unmeasured cost is never a pass — and the failure it exists for is specific: the cost walk goes launch by launch under a per-candidate RPC ceiling, so a budget that runs out part-way leaves a cost distribution describing only the launches walked FIRST, which are the newest ones. That is a biased sample rather than a short one, and a biased sample of a cost is a wrong number. 0.8 bounds the unpriced share to a fifth. THE CEILING COSTS WHOLE LAUNCHES AND NEVER HALF OF ONE, and that is enforced at BOTH ends rather than asserted: a launch is not started unless the remaining budget covers its whole target list, and — because that reservation cannot see retries or a re-asked null getTransaction, so the ceiling can still bite mid-walk — a launch that came back short is DISCARDED whole, its partial pricing dropped and the launch counted in entry.coverage.cost.launchesDiscarded (entry.coverage.cost.launchesSkippedForBudget is the other end: launches the reservation never started, on which nothing was spent). Without the second half the bias this bar exists to bound would reappear one level down, inside a launch, where a truncated walk holds the earliest entrants by slot. It is a floor on OUR coverage and not a property of any deployer, so falling below it yields entry-cost-unmeasured — an absence of a finding, never a finding of absence.
justification.minFieldHitRateGross: A NECESSARY CONDITION, NEVER A SUFFICIENT ONE, and it can only ever take a verdict away. The fill tape is gross of fees, so this rate is an upper bound: on our own subject's post-2026-06-04 launches the screen now reads 0.763 (351 of 460 closed round trips positive, over the 86 launches whose opening is proven; the superseded reading was 0.765 over 473, taken before unproven openings stopped being scored) while the fee-inclusive record puts the whole outsider population at +0.54 SOL per launch with 51 of 106 wallets negative. Below 0.5 the field loses money before costs and therefore certainly after them, which is conclusive; above it, nothing whatsoever is established. Stage 0 asserts that this leg cannot carry a positive verdict on its own.
justification.maxCandidatesScored: Stage 2 is the expensive leg per candidate — up to 144 keyless requests and about 17 minutes at the pinned 7s pacing — while Stage 1 costs one request per candidate. Scoring 3 of the gate's survivors bounds a full run at about 50 minutes worst case, and a typical one at about 17 minutes at the measured p50 of 4 pages; the committed elite run passed 5 of 12, so 3 is a real cap and the run reports how many survivors it dropped.
justification.maxLaunchesPerCandidate: Equal to minLaunchesSampled, so a candidate is either scored on a full sample or reported UNMEASURED. Sampling more would not sharpen the distribution enough to justify a proportional increase in the request bound, and sampling fewer could never clear the floor.
justification.maxRequestsPerLaunch: MEASURED from the committed tape's own build metadata, and the POPULATION MATTERS because the tape's windows are not all the same length. A live Stage 2 walk always reads a 60s window, and over the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000 the pages needed per launch run p50 4, p90 6, p95 6, MAX 13. The pooled figure across all 235 covered launches — p50 4, p90 8, p95 13, MAX 24 — is inflated by the 21 of them taped over 300s (and 4 over 120s), and it is what an earlier version of this entry quoted. The cap is on REQUESTS rather than pages because the endpoint sheds ~24.7% of what it is asked for (51,715 OK against 16,960 HTTP 429 on that same build) and the client retries; counting only successes would let a launch cost 3x the printed plan. At that shed rate a page costs ~1.33 requests, and a page is only STARTED when a whole 3-request page cost still fits (i.e. at spent <= 15), so 18 requests starts ABOUT 11-12 PAGES — not the 13-14 an earlier version claimed, which counted requests the loop will not spend. WHAT THAT COVERS, STATED EXACTLY RATHER THAN ROUNDED UP: 11-12 pages is roughly double the 60s p95 of 6, but it does NOT cover that population's observed maximum of 13 — the 2 launches in 210 (1.0%) that needed 13 pages would be dropped at the mean shed rate. That is the reported failure below, not a silent one, and it is why the value does not move: raising the cap to cover a 1% tail costs the whole 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 stage arithmetic. THE BOUND IS EXACT RATHER THAN APPROXIMATE: a page can cost up to 3 requests (one attempt plus two backoffs), so the walk reserves the WHOLE per-page cost before starting a page and a launch therefore costs at most 18 and never 20. Checking the cap only between pages would have let a walk with one request of headroom spend three, breaking the stage arithmetic the dry run prints as the entire exposure. THE TAIL IS DROPPED, NOT TRUNCATED SILENTLY: a launch that spends the cap without reaching the mint is reported as DROPPED with its own note, and the sampling bias is stated because the launches too busy to walk are exactly the interesting ones.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: swap-api.pump.fun, the fill walk, and only it. `budget.keylessMinIntervalMs` stays at 2000ms for frontend-api-v3, which has shed nothing here and must not be slowed for a fault on a different host. 7000ms is anchored on TWO INDEPENDENT READINGS OF THIS HOST. (i) LIVE: at 2000ms two consecutive Stage 2 runs against swap-api each lost 4 of the subject's 8 launches to HTTP 429 after all three attempts, so the run reported `entry-unmeasured` where the truth is `entry-room-absent`; the same code at 7000ms walked all 8 and produced `entry-room-absent`. A fast wrong answer is worth nothing, and the failure is silent in the direction that matters — a dropped launch degrades the verdict rather than announcing the pacing is wrong. (ii) THE TAPE BUILDER'S OWN RECORD against this same endpoint: the committed `window/*.meta.json` `delay` field — the adaptive delay each build settled on — reads p50 4.92s, p75 15s, p90 15.5s, max 40s, with only p10-p25 near 1.2s; and its shed share by delay quartile is 24.2% / 24.8% / 28.5% / 23.8% over the 238 builds carrying a stats block, i.e. 23.8-28.5% with the SLOWEST quartile no better than the fastest — an earlier version of this entry called that 'flat at ~24-25%', which understates the third quartile by ~4 points without changing what it establishes: backing off does not buy immunity and there is no cheap corner to sit in. 7s is therefore pinned deliberately between that p50 and p75 rather than at the bottom of the range. COST: the request arithmetic is untouched — 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 still — but the wall clock is not, so the typical run is about 17 minutes and the worst case about 50, and every printed estimate says so.
justification.keylessRetryBackoffMs: The tape build shed a quarter of its requests and its own recorded delay ranges from 0.75s to 40s, i.e. it backed off and retried through them. A client that treats a 429 as terminal cannot walk this endpoint at all - the first live check of the pager died on one, three launches in. Two retries at 3s and 9s clear the ordinary case, and EVERY attempt counts against both the per-launch cap and the stage ceiling, so a retry-heavy run gets a dropped launch rather than an unbounded one.
justification.tradePageLimit: 100 is what the trade endpoint serves per page and is the figure the AGENTS.md note is anchored on. Asking for less would multiply the request count for no benefit; the endpoint's own cap is what it is.
justification.windowMs: 60000 is the window_ms of 210 of the committed population tape's 239 launches — its MODAL window and not its only one: 25 were taped over 300000 and 4 over 120000, and calling it 'the tape's window_ms' (as an earlier version of this entry did) hides the 5x builds that inflate every page distribution measured across the whole tape (see maxRequestsPerLaunch). It is used for TWO things only: deciding a launch is old enough to have finished happening, and placing the seek cursor. It does NOT decide which fills are inside the measured window — windowSlotSpan does — because the mint time it would be measured from comes from the vendor and the fills come from pump.fun, and there is nothing to reconcile the two clocks with. BOTH OF THOSE TWO USES ARE windowMs + seekMarginMs, NOT windowMs ALONE, and stage2.mjs gates eligibility on the sum. The cursor was already placed at createdAtMs + windowMs + seekMarginMs while eligibility asked only for windowMs, so a launch aged 60-65s passed 'old enough to have finished happening' while the newest instant the walk reaches for had not happened yet — the same tail truncation seekMarginMs exists to prevent, arriving from the future side. The sum also covers the measured span (160 slots is 64.0s at the nominal 400ms/slot and ~63.5s observed), so the one gate covers both quantities and membership stays windowSlotSpan's alone. A test pins windowSlotSpan x 400ms <= windowMs + seekMarginMs so that widening the span past the gate fails loudly.
justification.windowSlotSpan: MEASURED, and deliberately NOT ceil(windowMs/400)=150, which is measurably too narrow. Across the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000 the observed slot span is p50 151, p75 153, p90 155, p95 155, MAX 158 — and 51% of them hold at least one fill beyond createSlot+150 (37.1% beyond 151, 5.2% beyond 155, 0.0% beyond 160). This is not a rounding nuisance: the trailing fills are disproportionately LATE SELLS, and dropping one flips a wallet from closed to open, which shrinks fieldClosedRoundTrips — itself a gate at minFieldRoundTrips 10. So a too-narrow span silently changes gate outcomes. 160 covers 100% of observed windows with margin over the observed max of 158. THE OTHER DIRECTION, ON THE RECORD RATHER THAN AS AN OBJECTION: at the tape's observed rate (60s <-> p50 151 slots, ~397ms/slot) 160 slots is ~63.5s, so the live window is up to ~3.5s WIDER than the tape's 60s windows, and the extra late sells make realised P&L read better than the ground-truth recipe would. Because the field leg is veto-only it loosens rather than tightens — a too-generous field can only fail to veto, never earn a verdict — and the magnitude is small. THAT MAGNITUDE CLAIM IS CITED, NOT MEASURED HERE: the figure behind it (the margin sits at the thinnest part of the window, p50 18 / p95 52 fills in the last 5s) is carried over from the PR #7 review comment that recorded this tradeoff, which supplied it without naming a population, and it is reproduced nowhere in this repo — unlike the span figures above, which name theirs (the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000). 160 was chosen on measurement, so no change is implied. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH ELIGIBILITY: the span is no longer what decides a launch is old enough to measure — stage2.mjs gates on windowMs + seekMarginMs (65s), which dominates this span at both the nominal 400ms/slot (64.0s) and the observed rate, so widening the span towards 65s would eat that margin and past it would break the gate, which a test pins. STAGE 0 DELIBERATELY DOES NOT USE THIS: it measures each committed launch over its own stored window, because the 1,502-pair reproduction against wallet_launch_pnl.csv is computed that way and that regression guard is not traded for cosmetic consistency between the two paths.
justification.seekMarginMs: The walk seeks from createdAtMs + windowMs + this, so a vendor mint time running EARLY by less than 5s cannot cut the tail off the window before the slot trim ever sees it. It replaces a tail-truncation detector that could not discriminate — launches simply stop trading before the nominal window end (p50 observed span 151 against a 160 span), so any such detector fires on nearly every launch and carries no information. Designing the failure out beats reporting it. COST: the walk still pages BACKWARDS to the mint and still trims by slot afterwards, so the margin only adds rows at the newest end — about 5s of trading, roughly 30 fills at a p50 of 362 fills per window over the 210 launches taped at 60s — the population a live walk matches; pooled across all 235 covered launches the p50 is 381 and the answer is the same — i.e. at most one extra page of 100. maxRequestsPerLaunch is 18, about 11-12 STARTED pages at the measured shed rate against a p95 of 6 pages over the 210 launches taped at this window length, so that one extra page fits inside the existing cap for all but the same 1% tail the cap already drops and reports and the 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 stage arithmetic is unchanged. IT ALSO BOUNDS ELIGIBILITY, because it must: stage2.mjs skips a launch younger than windowMs + seekMarginMs, since the cursor this margin places is the newest instant the walk reaches for and a launch aged 60-65s has not got there yet. THIS IS A CURSOR HINT AND NOT A TOLERANCE: the pre-mint tripwire still compares ts < createdAtMs with ZERO slack (the measured gap is exactly 0 on all 235 committed launches) and coverage is still discharged only by the endpoint explicitly saying nothing older exists.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: Stage 2's own sub-ceiling, enforced on its own client so it cannot eat the --consistency pass's budget. 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 is the exact declared worst case, so no plan-level truncation is possible: the ceiling and the plan agree, and the dry run prints both. Typical cost is far lower - at the measured p50 of 4 pages plus shedding it is about 6 requests a launch, so roughly 144 for a full run. At the pinned 7s pacing for this host that is about 17 minutes typical against about 50 minutes worst case, and the run prints both so an operator does not mistake a slow walk for a hang. A launch is only started when a full per-launch cap of headroom remains, so a run can never abandon a launch half-walked.

$comment: THE PRICE OF THE SEAT. Captain's standing ruling, 2026-08-02: fees are part of the entry
window, and 'enterable' means enterable AFTER what it costs to enter. Captain decision 136b
adds the field's AFTER-COST result, which is what stops the field leg being veto-only.
Keyless, and it spends NO vendor quota — it is Solana RPC, on the same host and the same
pacing as the creation walk. It spends no swap-api request either: every signature it prices
came free with a fill Stage 2 had already parsed.
IT RUNS ONLY WHEN THE FREE LEGS HAVE NOT ALREADY REFUSED. Room and the gross field are
arithmetic over fills in hand, so they are scored first; a deployer that fails either costs
zero RPC requests. That ordering is the whole cost model.
WHAT IT CANNOT SEE, and it must travel with every number this block produces: a landing tip
paid in a SEPARATE transaction of the same bundle is not recoverable from the entrant's own
transaction and is not measured anywhere in this repo's ground truth either. Its absence
biases the answer OPTIMISTICALLY — entry looks cheaper, and the field more profitable, than
either was. So the cost leg is a GATE and never a pass.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: MEASURED from the committed tape, re-derived 2026-08-02 rather than copied. Distinct transactions per launch, over the 235 covered launches: the create-slot scope reads p50 7, p90 13, MAX 20 (post-break p50 7, p90 12, max 14); the whole-window scope over CLOSED create-slot outsiders reads p50 18, p90 35, MAX 70 (post-break p50 19, p90 28, max 70). The two scopes are UNIONED before anything is fetched, so a closed entrant's create-slot transaction is paid for once, AND THE UNION IS WHAT MUST BE COSTED: re-running entryCostTargets as the code calls it over those 235 launches gives p50 19, p90 36.6, MAX 74 distinct transactions per launch — not 7 + 18. At maxLaunchesPerCandidate 8 that is about 152 requests at the median, ~293 at p90 and ~592 at the observed worst. An earlier version of this entry printed 200 / 380 / 700, which is the same arithmetic with the union left out (the plain sums 25 / 48 / 90 x 8); it overstated the cost by ~30% and the conclusion below survives under either reading. 400 covers the median and the p90 whole and truncates only a pathological candidate, and it truncates VISIBLY: a launch is never priced half-way, so the ceiling costs whole launches and entry.coverage.cost records how many. At the pinned 2.5s that is about 6 minutes per candidate at the median (152 requests; the ~8 an earlier version printed was the un-unioned 200) and about 17 at the ceiling; with maxCandidatesScored 3 the declared worst case is 3 x 400 = 1,200 requests and about 50 minutes, which the dry run prints. The realistic cost is far lower because only candidates that survive room AND the gross field are priced at all — the committed live run had one such candidate of three.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: INHERITED FROM creation_walk.rpcMinIntervalMs AND NOT AN INDEPENDENT CHOICE — api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress, getTransaction and getBlock, so this leg and the creation walk draw on one allowance. 2,500ms is that block's measured figure: 1,400ms is the documented floor but a 200-request run at that pace took over 890 seconds instead of 280 because the endpoint was shedding and the backoff was paying for it. The two legs are SERIALISED rather than run beside each other for the same reason: two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout. Batching is not used here either — measured actively harmful on this host, 58s at batch=1 with zero shed events against 110s at batch=8 with eleven.
justification.preferBlockRoute: getBlock(slot, transactionDetails='full') returns EVERY transaction in the create slot in one request, collapsing the create-slot scope from ~7 requests a launch to 1. It is UNTESTED against this endpoint from this repo — what is known is that getBlock works here for signature listing; what is unknown is whether the public endpoint serves full blocks to this client and what a busy mainnet slot's payload costs. So it is probed BEHIND A FALLBACK: anything other than a usable block latches the candidate onto the per-signature route, and the route that ran reaches the run record so a saved run says which one paid for its numbers. It buys request count and NOTHING ELSE — in particular it does not reach out-of-transaction landing tips, because attributing a sibling transaction in the same slot to the same bundle is an inference the chain does not support. Set false to pin the walk to the proven route.
